Olawepo-Hashim condemns attack on Sowore, warns against political violence  The Accord Party presidential candidate, Dr Gbenga Olawepo-Hashim, has condemned the growing threat of political violence in Nigeria, warning that a country already grappling with terrorism, banditry, kidnapping and other security challenges cannot afford politically motivated attacks.  Hashim gave the warning during a solidarity visit to the African Action Congress (AAC) presidential candidate and human rights activist, Omoyele Sowore, following an attack on him in Ekiti State.  “Nigeria cannot afford to add political violence to the general insecurity in the land,” Hashim said, stressing that attacks on political actors threaten democratic freedoms and national stability.  The Accord Party candidate welcomed a statement by a United Nations representative expressing concern over the incident but urged other international partners to speak out, insisting that political violence must attract clear and consistent condemnation.  He also called on President Bola Tinubu to caution members of his team against rhetoric and actions capable of provoking political confrontation.  “The President should call his team to order. They should not provoke war because they would be the first to run away,” he said.  The visit also highlighted the longstanding relationship between the two pro-democracy activists, dating back to their involvement in the struggle against military rule.  Describing Sowore as a comrade from the early days of the struggle, Hashim said, “Sowore is our own. We brought him into the movement in 1989/1990.”  In his response, Sowore expressed appreciation for the solidarity visit, describing Hashim as a senior comrade who introduced him to political activism at the University of Lagos.  “I am most grateful for this solidarity visit by my senior comrade and colleague, presidential candidate of the Accord Party. He was one of those who brought me into the struggle in UNILAG. We fought against military rule together when some people ran away,” Sowore said.  He maintained that the attack would neither intimidate him nor weaken his commitment to the struggle for democracy.  “We are not intimidated, and we shall continue to fight until genuine democracy is established,” he added.  The visit underscored the longstanding bond between the two activists and their shared position that political disagreements should not be used to justify violence.

Severe weather has affected communities across the Navajo Nation, with impacts reported in Chinle, Birdsprings and Rock Point, Arizona; Sheep Springs and Shiprock, New Mexico; and Bluff, Utah.    Following the first round of weather impacts, the Navajo Nation Emergency Operations Center was activated on September 17. After additional weather systems affected the region, the Navajo Nation Risk Coordinator requested support from our Southwest Geographic Area. In coordination with the Bureau of Indian Affairs Office of Emergency Management, an Ad Hoc Type 3 Incident Management Team was mobilized. The team inbriefed with the Navajo Nation EOC on November 3.    The team is integrating with EOC staff to provide incident management support, technical assistance and training to strengthen emergency response capabilities.    The same weather systems also affected the White Mountain Apache Tribe and Hopi, both within the Southwest's Little Colorado River Unit. Similar support efforts are underway with the White Mountain Apache Tribe.    This response demonstrates how our wildland fire personnel apply their incident management expertise in partnership with Native communities during emergencies beyond wildfire.

Belarusian Intelligence Recruitment in Poland: From Proxy Networks to NATO Infrastructure Threats  The central security problem is the use of low-cost, locally recruited intermediaries to translate foreign intelligence requirements into activity inside European territory, potentially progressing from information collection and propaganda to operational reconnaissance, sabotage preparation and physical attacks.  Polish prosecutorial records establish that recruitment through digital messaging platforms, compensated photographic assignments, propaganda distribution and preparation for subsequent instructions have already occurred in investigations involving foreign intelligence activity. A 2 July 2026 prosecution announcement described recruitment through Telegram, photographic documentation of critical infrastructure, posters, graffiti and cryptocurrency payments. National Public Prosecutor’s Office — 2 July 2026.  A separate February 2026 investigation identified suspected Belarusian military intelligence activity across Poland, Germany and Lithuania, concerning critical infrastructure and facilities relevant to NATO defence. National Public Prosecutor’s Office — 23 February 2026.  The operational consequences are demonstrated by documented Russian-directed sabotage investigations. Polish prosecutors attributed the May 2024 Marywilska 44 commercial-centre fire to an organised operation conducted on behalf of Russian intelligence, while the November 2025 railway attacks created an immediate danger of a train disaster. National Public Prosecutor’s Office — 2 April 2026; National Public Prosecutor’s Office — 19 November 2025.  Principal judgment: The verified pattern establishes a credible counterintelligence threat to Poland and allied states. However, the identity, command structure and operational scale of any newly reported Belarusian KGB recruitment campaign must be distinguished from the already documented cases. The public official records examined do not independently establish that every reported leaflet assignment originates from the Belarusian KGB.  Decision consequence: Effective prevention requires detecting the transition from ostensibly minor paid assignments to intelligence-directed activity, protecting strategically consequential infrastructure, maintaining legally proportionate investigative powers and strengthening cross-border intelligence cooperation without treating nationality or migration status as evidence of hostile activity.  Belarusian Intelligence, Russian Sabotage and Europe’s Hidden Infrastructure Vulnerability: The Cost of Defending NATO from Within Europe is strengthening its eastern borders while foreign intelligence networks have demonstrated the ability to operate inside the civilian infrastructure on which its defence depends. Poland’s response exposes the contradiction: approximately PLN 10 billion committed to the Eastern Shield programme for 2024–2028, while Russian-directed networks have been prosecuted for espionage, commercial arson and attacks on railway infrastructure. Belarusian intelligence investigations now extend across Poland, Germany and Lithuania. The threat is no longer defined exclusively by hostile forces approaching NATO territory, but by the ability of foreign services to exploit civilian access, digital communications and infrastructure dependencies within it. The governing security question is whether European governments can convert legal authority, counterintelligence and infrastructure investment into effective prevention before relatively inexpensive clandestine operations impose disproportionate economic, military and political costs.  The financial imbalance is becoming a defence problem The figures illustrate the asymmetry. Poland’s Eastern Shield programme carries a planned financial envelope of approximately PLN 10 billion over 2024–2028, intended to strengthen border defence, detection, warning and military-support infrastructure. Yet Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) has disclosed a Russian-directed intelligence network comprising at least 30 individuals, including an original group of 16 detained participants subsequently reported convicted. The network combined reconnaissance, propaganda activity and preparations for more serious operations. Its strength was not a conventional military capability but its ability to organise dispersed tasks through intermediaries already present in Poland. Eastern Shield — Polish Government, June 2024; Camera-Network Investigation — ABW.  The military implications are measurable. On 23 November 2025, NATO reported that its Polish logistical hub supporting Ukraine handled approximately 18,000 tonnes of material per month. This is reported operational throughput, not maximum capacity or total assistance delivered through Poland. Nevertheless, it establishes the scale of an allied logistical function dependent on transport infrastructure, communications, personnel and supporting services. The destruction or interruption of one supporting service need not eliminate the entire operation to impose additional costs, delays and security requirements. The actual consequences would depend on redundancy, inventory and restoration capacity—variables not quantified in the published record. NATO Logistics Hub in Poland — NATO, November 2025.  The European Union has also recognised the problem institutionally. Its proposed Military Mobility Package of November 2025 envisages an EU-wide military mobility area by 2027, including measures to simplify procedures and improve cross-border movement. The proposal identifies administrative and infrastructure constraints affecting military transport; it does not establish that the projected system is already operational. Europe’s defence ambitions therefore remain dependent on civilian transport capacity and the implementation of national and European measures whose costs cannot be assessed solely through military procurement budgets. Military Mobility Package — European Commission, November 2025.  A commercial warehouse can become an instrument of geopolitical pressure The investigation into the 12 May 2024 fire at Warsaw’s Marywilska 44 commercial centre demonstrates how economic infrastructure can become a target of foreign intelligence-directed sabotage without possessing an explicit military function. Polish prosecutors attributed the arson to an organised group acting on behalf of Russian intelligence. Their April 2026 announcement nevertheless acknowledged that the individuals who directly ignited the fire had not been identified. Organisational attribution and identification of direct perpetrators are separate evidentiary conclusions. Commercial Arson Indictment — Polish National Public Prosecutor’s Office, April 2026.  The investigation extended beyond Marywilska 44. Prosecutors identified the 13–14 April 2024 fire at an OBI store in Warsaw, the 9 May 2024 IKEA fire in Vilnius and preparations for another operation at an IKEA facility in Riga. The Riga attack was not completed. On 25 March 2026, prosecutors filed an indictment against five individuals associated with the wider proceedings. The geographical distribution is consequential: attacks, suspected organisers, evidence and judicial responsibilities can span several states, while commercial operators bear the immediate consequences in the jurisdictions where destruction occurs. Commercial Arson Indictment — Polish National Public Prosecutor’s Office, April 2026.  Such destruction affects more than the value of damaged premises. Retailers, tenants, employees, insurers, suppliers and transport providers face different forms of exposure. Reconstruction costs, business interruption, employment consequences and emergency expenditure cannot be consolidated into a credible economic-loss estimate without audited evidence. The prosecution also described efforts to record fires and emergency-service responses for propaganda purposes. Physical damage could therefore serve a second function: producing material intended to extend the political effect beyond the immediate commercial loss. The available evidence establishes that alleged objective, not the scale of any resulting change in public opinion. Marywilska 44 Investigation — Polish National Public Prosecutor’s Office, May 2025.  The railway attacks exposed the limits of conventional infrastructure protection The 15–16 November 2025 incidents affecting Poland’s railway Line 7 marked another form of escalation. Prosecutors described explosive damage near Mika and interference with railway infrastructure near Gołąb, creating an immediate danger of railway catastrophe. Two Ukrainian citizens were accused of carrying out the attacks for Russian intelligence and subsequently fleeing to Belarus. The prosecutorial attribution concerns Russian intelligence; the suspects’ nationality and reported destination do not independently establish Belarusian KGB command. Railway Sabotage Investigation — Polish National Public Prosecutor’s Office, November 2025.  Railway infrastructure illustrates the economic difference between destroying an asset and interrupting a service. Transport continuity depends on tracks, signalling, communications, traction systems, safety inspections and operational authorisations. A physically limited incident may require wider restrictions until safe movement is restored. Its consequences depend on the duration of interruption and the availability of alternative services, not simply the cost of replacing damaged equipment. The railway investigation established serious safety implications, but the published prosecution record does not quantify destroyed military shipments, national freight losses or a measurable reduction in NATO readiness. Those distinctions determine whether government spending addresses demonstrated vulnerabilities or politically compelling but unverified assumptions.  The European Union’s Critical Entities Resilience Directive (EU) 2022/2557 addresses this wider dependency problem across 11 sectors, including energy, transport, health, water, digital infrastructure and food-related activities. Member states were required to identify critical entities under the directive’s framework by July 2026. The significance is regulatory: a facility’s economic and security relevance depends increasingly on the essential services it provides and on other systems relying upon them. Identification and legal compliance, however, do not guarantee operational continuity under attack. Critical Infrastructure Resilience — European Commission, January 2026.  Minsk and Moscow share interests, but attribution cannot be politically convenient The intelligence relationship between Belarus and Russia requires particular precision. Polish proceedings establish different institutional categories: activity attributed to the Belarusian State Security Committee, commonly known as the KGB; activity attributed to Belarusian military intelligence; and Russian-directed networks employing individuals of several nationalities. Their strategic interests may overlap, but public evidence does not establish that every operation is governed by a unified command structure.  A particularly consequential case emerged on 9 February 2026, when Poland’s ABW arrested Pavel T., a Belarusian citizen suspected of conducting reconnaissance for Belarusian military intelligence between June 2024 and February 2026. The alleged activity extended across Poland, Germany and Lithuania, involving critical infrastructure and facilities relevant to Polish and NATO defence. German and Lithuanian intelligence authorities cooperated with Poland in the investigation. The case demonstrates that the institutional concern extends beyond Belarusian opposition communities, but remains an allegation subject to judicial proceedings. Belarusian Military Intelligence Investigation — Polish National Public Prosecutor’s Office, February 2026.  The distinction has financial and diplomatic consequences. Sanctions, criminal prosecutions and bilateral intelligence cooperation depend on identifying the relevant actors and their conduct. On 8 October 2026, the Council of the European Union extended restrictive measures against Russian destabilising activities until 9 October 2027, covering 80 individuals and 20 entities. These listings impose defined financial and travel restrictions; they do not constitute criminal convictions or establish responsibility for every incident in Poland. Incorrectly merging Russian and Belarusian institutional attribution would weaken the evidentiary foundation on which such measures are justified. Russian Hybrid Activities: Restrictive Measures — Council of the EU, October 2026.  Stronger criminal law cannot replace faster, legally admissible evidence Poland’s 17 August 2023 reform of Article 130 of its Criminal Code expanded the statutory treatment of foreign intelligence activity, including preparatory conduct and sabotage-related offences. Under Article 130 §7, specified sabotage or terrorism-related conduct undertaken for foreign intelligence carries imprisonment for at least ten years or life; §8 separately addresses qualifying preparation. The legislation creates grounds for intervention before completed destruction in defined circumstances, but it does not eliminate the obligation to establish the offence and respect criminal-procedure safeguards. Polish Criminal Code Amendment — August 2023.  A further reform entered into force on 31 October 2026, strengthening judicial oversight of operational surveillance conducted by authorised Polish services. Courts receive additional supervisory powers concerning the conduct and results of surveillance. The reform arrived as digital communications and cross-border financial records were becoming central to the investigation of clandestine activity. Greater investigative capability and stronger oversight are not necessarily opposing objectives: unlawfully collected evidence can compromise prosecution, while inadequate safeguards can weaken public confidence and cooperation. Judicial Oversight of Operational Surveillance — Polish Legislation, September 2026.  At EU level, Regulation (EU) 2023/1543 became applicable on 18 August 2026, establishing European Production and Preservation Orders for specified electronic evidence. The framework provides a general ten-day response period for covered production orders and eight hours in qualifying emergencies. These are legal deadlines, not observed average processing times. Together with financial-transfer traceability under Regulation (EU) 2023/1113, applicable since 30 December 2024, the instruments can strengthen lawful access to certain forms of evidence. They cannot, without corroboration, prove that a payment or online account belongs to a foreign intelligence organisation. EU e-Evidence Framework — European Commission; Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 — European Parliament and Council.  Europe has common obligations but no single authority responsible for the entire threat Poland and Lithuania confront the geographical consequences of proximity to Belarus; Germany contributes allied logistics and military coordination through NATO’s NSATU headquarters in Wiesbaden; Italy’s obligations include implementation of NIS2 through Legislative Decree No. 138 of 4 September 2024; France’s National Strategic Review 2025 identifies hostile interference and resilience as national-security concerns; and the United Kingdom’s Strategic Defence Review 2025 connects critical infrastructure protection to military effectiveness. These are different national responsibilities, not interchangeable security models. Italian Legislative Decree 138/2024 — Normattiva; French National Strategic Review 2025 — SGDSN; UK Strategic Defence Review 2025 — Ministry of Defence.  NATO’s North Atlantic Treaty reinforces the distinction. Article 3 concerns the capacity to resist armed attack, Article 4 provides for security consultations, and Article 5 establishes collective defence under specified conditions. An intelligence-directed sabotage incident does not automatically trigger Article 5. National authorities remain responsible for criminal investigations and relevant infrastructure protection, while NATO addresses allied defence and preparedness. The European Union contributes regulatory obligations, judicial cooperation, financial restrictions and military-mobility initiatives within its own competences. The North Atlantic Treaty — NATO, April 1949.  The unresolved institutional problem is implementation across those boundaries. EU rules may improve financial traceability, but intelligence attribution still depends on investigators. NATO can coordinate military requirements, but civilian infrastructure is operated under national and commercial arrangements. The forthcoming direct supervisory responsibilities of the EU’s Anti-Money Laundering Authority, scheduled to begin for selected institutions in 2028, will add another financial supervisory capability, not a substitute for national counterintelligence. The effectiveness of European coordination will therefore depend on evidence exchange, clearly assigned responsibilities and actual service continuity rather than the number of authorities involved. EU Anti-Money Laundering Package — Council of the EU, May 2024.  The next 24 months will reveal who absorbs the cost Between November 2026 and November 2028, European governments face a measurable implementation test. Poland’s Eastern Shield programme will approach its planned 2028 completion horizon; the EU’s proposed military-mobility architecture carries a 2027 objective; newly applicable electronic-evidence rules must demonstrate operational results; and AMLA is scheduled to begin direct supervision of selected financial institutions in 2028. None of these milestones, taken alone, establishes that essential infrastructure is safer or hostile networks easier to disrupt.  The costs of inadequate implementation will fall first on infrastructure operators, whose investment, insurance, restoration and compliance obligations are not automatically reimbursed by defence budgets. Businesses and employees will bear the commercial consequences of interruption. Transport users and logistics providers will absorb delays and additional operating costs. National governments will face emergency expenditure, investigative burdens and pressure to strengthen protection. Allied defence institutions may encounter additional constraints where civilian services supporting military requirements are affected. The distribution of those costs cannot be quantified from the published record, but the transmission mechanisms are identifiable.  There is also a political and legal cost. Belarusian opposition communities and Ukrainian residents cannot be treated collectively as intelligence risks because individuals from those nationalities appear in criminal investigations. Such an approach would undermine lawful cooperation and potentially discourage reporting of coercion. The Council of Europe’s Resolution 2669 of 25 June 2026, addressing transnational repression, reinforces the need for protective reporting mechanisms and proportionate state responses. The security value of credible community cooperation belongs in the same institutional calculation as surveillance authority and criminal prosecution. Fighting Back against Transnational Repression — Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, June 2026.  By November 2028, the relevant measure of progress will not be the volume of public warnings or the severity of announced penalties. It will be whether Poland and its European partners can demonstrate faster lawful evidence acquisition, more reliable identification of foreign intelligence direction, effective interruption of serious preparations and documented continuity of essential services. The cost of failing that test will be borne by taxpayers, infrastructure companies, workers and allied logistical systems—not by the organisations that can commission an operation remotely and leave European institutions to finance its consequences. debuglies.com/2026/11/06/bel… via @https://debuglies.com

The fact that Mercado Bitcoin publicly announced the breach was contained while thousands of customer deposit addresses continued to be systematically drained for hours afterward raises serious questions about their real-time monitoring and incident response.    On-chain analysis (especially from Bitquery) shows roughly 36,000 Ethereum deposit addresses were emptied even after the “all clear,” with total losses estimated between $36M and nearly $49M across 10–11 chains. While the exchange has promised full reimbursement from its own reserves, incidents like this strongly reinforce why self-custody is still the only reliable way to protect meaningful amounts of crypto.    Stay safe and vigilant!

Claude Dispatch의 'ThisBash'.  공격은 다음 순서로 진행된다.  ㄱ) 확장 프로그램이 claude.ai의 로그인 세션에 접근 ㄴ) Dispatch API에서 연결된 Desktop 세션 탐색 ㄷ) Claude에게 명령을 반복 전달 ㄹ) 응답에 맞춰 후속 프롬프트로 실행 유도 ㅁ) Allow 버튼까지 자동 클릭 ㅂ) Desktop에서 로컬 코드 실행  이른바 'Prompt Forcing'이다. AI의 응답을 읽고 다음 지시를 조정해 거부를 극복하는 방식이다.  연구자는 악성 npm 패키지 설치 후 계산기를 실행하는 PoC로 이를 입증했다. 실제 악성코드 감염 사례를 확인한 것은 아니다.  더 심각한 문제는 기기 간 연결이다.  개인 PC의 브라우저 확장이 동일 계정으로 연결된 회사 PC의 Desktop까지 접근할 수 있다면, 개인 환경이 기업 침투 경로가 될 수 있다.  Anthropic은 5월 14일 제보를 받고 5월 19일 취약점을 인정했지만 기존 이슈와 중복이라며 종결했다. 10월 말 Dispatch 종료를 계획했지만 11월 5일 보도 당시 기존 이용자는 계속 사용할 수 있었다.  핵심은 웹 로그인 인증이 PC의 명령 실행 권한으로 이어졌다는 점이다.  AI 에이전트의 편리한 기기 연결과 실행 권한은 어디까지 분리해야 할까?  #AI보안 #사이버보안 #Claude

ThreatMon’s latest report examines 10 significant ransomware cases and the activities of five threat groups: Qilin, Booba Project, Safepay, Nightspire, and Thegentlemen. 🚨 Threat Actor Claims Massive Breach of AU Small Finance Bank, Alleging 1.2 TB Data Leak  A threat actor has posted a claim on an underground forum alleging a significant data breach at AU Small Finance Bank, one of India's leading small finance banks. The actor claims to have compromised the bank's full database and is offering the stolen data for sale for $8,500. The post directly contradicts the bank's official statement issued in late October 2026, which attributed the incident to a limited data leak involving a third-party Salesforce SaaS platform affecting only vehicle loan customers.  The actor alleges that the bank's own core systems were breached, not just the external SaaS platform. According to the forum post, the stolen dataset totals 1.2 TB and contains over 1 billion records. The actor claims the bank is downplaying the severity of the incident to avoid regulatory scrutiny and customer panic.  The alleged compromised data includes: - 3,846,888 complete KYC identity records containing PAN, Aadhaar numbers, dates of birth, mobile numbers, emails, full addresses, and family names - 2,282,619 live customer accounts - 1,917,657 exposed bank account numbers - 938,403,770 core banking transaction and servicing records - 30,266,393 credit bureau, CIBIL, and FICO risk dossiers - 72,241,539 loan book, collateral, sanction, and insurance records - 2,871,796 signed loan agreements, scanned cheques, and customer signatures  AU Small Finance Bank, headquartered in Chennai, serves millions of customers across India with a focus on financial inclusion. The exposure of Aadhaar numbers and PAN details poses severe risks of identity theft and financial fraud for the affected individuals. The actor also provided links to sample files hosted on various file-sharing services to verify the authenticity of the dump.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified. While the bank has acknowledged a security incident related to a third-party platform, the extent of the compromise claimed by the threat actor remains unconfirmed by independent security researchers or regulatory bodies.

⚠️Threat Actor Claims 103 GB Hilton Hotel Breach on Underground Forum  A threat actor known as "BigBrother" has posted a claim on an underground forum alleging a significant data breach affecting Hilton Hotels. The post, dated November 5, 2026, asserts that the actor has compromised the hotel chain's central server, resulting in the exposure of 103 GB of data containing approximately 7,394,423 rows of customer information.  According to the listing, the stolen dataset includes personal data from Hilton Hotels customers. The actor alleges that this is their first time breaching or leaking such a target and provides a session hash as proof of access. The post does not specify the exact types of Personal Identifiable Information (PII) contained within the rows, though previous posts by this actor have involved large-scale PII dumps including national IDs and financial records.  The threat actor's track record suggests a pattern of targeting large organizations with high-value data. In September 2026, the same individual posted claims regarding massive PII leaks from Iranian institutions, including Al-Mustafa International University (89,000 records), Samaneh Khodnevis (23 million records), and HAMTA (62 million records). These prior posts were accompanied by screenshots and CSV samples, indicating a consistent methodology of offering data for sale in Bitcoin.  Hilton Worldwide is one of the largest hospitality companies globally, operating over 8,000 hotels and resorts across more than 120 countries. A breach of this magnitude, if verified, would expose sensitive guest data to potential identity theft and fraud. At the time of reporting, Hilton has not publicly confirmed the incident, and the alleged breach has not been independently verified.

🚨Moondancer Ransomware Claims Compunet Breach, Exposes 59M Rows of Mitsubishi Data  The Moondancer ransomware group has claimed responsibility for a significant cyberattack on Compunet S.A., a Colombian IT services provider, resulting in the alleged exposure of sensitive data belonging to its client, Mitsubishi Electric Colombia. According to a post on the Darkforums underground platform, the threat actor collaborated with a partner group to publish CSV dumps from Compunet’s ERP system, which reportedly contain 59 million rows and 110,000 invoices.  The post alleges that the attackers compromised more than 30 ESXi hosts and 270 virtual machines within Compunet’s infrastructure. The group claims to have encrypted 270 TB of data and deleted 60 TB of backups after negotiations with Compunet failed. The ransom note displayed in the thread addresses the CEO of Compunet directly, demanding payment or facing further data leaks.  The incident reportedly affected multiple other clients of Compunet, including: * Adama * SierraCol * Freskaleche * Ciamsa * Nutriavicola  The threat actor stated that data from these additional companies had already been sold to a private client and would not be published publicly. Compunet is a major IT solutions provider in Colombia, serving various industrial and corporate sectors. If authentic, the breach could expose operational data and financial records for numerous manufacturing and agricultural entities in the region.  At the time of reporting, neither Compunet nor Mitsubishi Electric Colombia has independently confirmed the breach or the extent of the data exposure.  #Ransomware #Moondancer #Compunet #MitsubishiElectric #DataLeak #CyberSecurity #DarkWeb

🚨 Threat Actor Claims iOS 27 Zero-Click RCE Exploit for Sale on Darkweb  A listing on an underground forum claims the availability of a zero-day remote code execution (RCE) exploit targeting Apple's upcoming iOS 27 operating system. The post, dated November 4, 2026, alleges that the vulnerability allows for root-level privilege escalation via a crafted iMessage payload without any user interaction, classifying it as a Zero-Click attack.  According to the thread, the exploit is purportedly compatible with modern iPhones and iPads running iOS 27.2 and upcoming updates. The seller describes the exploit as "very expensive" and states that only genuine buyers should make contact. While the post does not provide technical proof-of-concept (PoC) details or screenshots of the exploit in action, it explicitly mentions that escrow services are accepted for transactions.  The threat actor behind the listing has not been independently identified in this specific thread, and no prior track record was provided in the source material to verify their reputation or past activities. Claims of zero-day exploits for major mobile operating systems are frequently used as bait in underground markets; therefore, the authenticity of this specific iOS 27 vulnerability remains unverified.  If authentic, a zero-click RCE with root privileges would represent a critical security risk, potentially enabling state-sponsored actors or advanced cybercriminals to spy on high-value targets or install persistent malware undetected. At the time of reporting, Apple has not acknowledged the existence of this specific vulnerability, and the claim has not been independently verified by security researchers.  #iOS27 #ZeroDayExploit #AppleSecurity #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity

🚨 Threat Actor Claims 26GB Database Breach of Argentina Federal Police  A darkweb forum post alleges that the threat actor known as SkyLing, operating under the banner of MortemTeam, has compromised the database of the Argentine Federal Police (Policía Federal Argentina, PFA). According to the listing, the actor claims to have exfiltrated a dataset totaling 26 GB from the law enforcement agency. The post, dated November 4, 2026, includes a taunting message directed at the Argentine government, stating that continued neglect of system security will result in further data exposure.  The Argentine Federal Police is a national law enforcement agency responsible for federal crimes, border control, and public order in major urban centers. As a critical government entity, it holds sensitive data related to criminal investigations, citizen records, and operational intelligence. If authentic, the exposure of such a large volume of data could potentially compromise ongoing investigations and expose personal information of citizens or personnel involved in federal cases.  SkyLing has been active on underground forums recently, targeting various government and institutional entities in Latin America. The actor’s track record includes alleged breaches of the University of Buenos Aires, the Municipality of Moreno in Argentina, and state government bodies in Mexico. In previous posts, SkyLing claimed to have dumped student records, vehicle registration data, and sensitive information from gender-based violence attention centers, often citing weak credentials or unpatched systems as the entry vector. This pattern suggests a focus on low-hanging fruit within public sector infrastructure across the region.  At the time of reporting, the Argentine Federal Police has not publicly confirmed the breach, and the authenticity of the claimed 26 GB dataset remains unverified.

Beget recovery update: 60% of shared hosting restored after destructive attack  Russian hosting provider Beget says recovery continues after the Nov 1–2 destructive attack that wiped VPS, S3 and Kubernetes data. In a Nov 5 status update it reported:  • 60% of shared-hosting servers back online (up from 35% on Nov 4) • 40% of managed dedicated servers restored (up from 15%) • 100% of unmanaged dedicated servers already running • Most VPS file-level backups survived; restoring backup servers ~24 hours, then control-panel access estimated at about five days • Billing paused while services remain unrestored  This is a material recovery UPDATE to the earlier attack, not a new incident.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Figures and timelines are Beget's own estimates, not guarantees. Hard-hit servers still need rebuilds from backups with no firm ETA. Ransomware has not been established; Beget described deletion scripts after management-plane access. Independent coverage of the same update: 1prime.ru.  t.me/beget_official/579 #CyberSecurity #CloudSecurity #IncidentResponse

🚨 RUBY ON RAILS: CRITICAL ACTIVE STORAGE FLAW (CVSS 9.8) ALLOWS UNAUTHENTICATED FILE WRITE VIA IMAGE UPLOADS  Rails has disclosed a critical flaw in Active Storage. Apps that process uploads with ImageMagick may let an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the server with one crafted upload.  • Advisory: GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (no CVE yet), CVSS 9.8 • Attaching the file is enough; no variant, preview or analyze call is needed • With the Disk service, attackers may also read any file the app can read, including secret_key_base and credentials • Fixed in activestorage 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Rails does not say whether the flaw has been exploited. Upgrade now. If you store attachments with the Disk service, rotate secret_key_base, the master key and every credential the app can read.  github.com/rails/rails/secur… #DDW #DarkWeb #RubyOnRails #AppSec #PatchNow

Backdoored ARTEX Docker images pulled from Docker Hub, but installs stay at risk ⚠️  BadByte says a trojanized image of ARTEX, the AI-driven penetration testing console abused in recent bank attacks, gave anyone who knew the trick a root shell. Commands sent through the login form's captcha field ran before the password was checked.  • 7,946 pulls of tomicdd/artex and congdonglinux/artex before disclosure • 46 of 62 exposed consoles still served the backdoored build on Nov 4 • 637 GitHub repos still pointed their compose file at it • Docker removed both images on Nov 5  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Removal does not clean existing installs: any copy already pulled or cached on a mirror is still backdoored. U.S. agencies warn of attacks on cold-chain systems ⚠️  CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DoT say they are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems globally, including electronic temperature and commercial refrigeration controllers used in retail grocery and cold storage.  The joint Cybersecurity Advisory (as of Nov 5, 2026) warns that actors may exploit authentication bypass, code injection or weak configurations on unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to alter setpoints, force continuous heating/defrost cycles, cause inventory loss and equipment hazards, or create a denial-of-view condition. Healthcare, chemical, food and agriculture, and transportation sectors are named as heavy users of these systems.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: This is an official warning of ongoing malicious activity; it does not identify an actor or establish a new incident today. It follows earlier European supermarket and cold-room refrigeration tampering reported in October–early November 2026. Operators should remove unnecessary internet exposure, secure any required remote access, isolate OT networks, change default credentials, patch firmware and alert on setpoint deviations.  ic3.gov/CSA/2026/261105.pdf #CyberSecurity #OTSecurity #ICS #CriticalInfrastructure

Firecracker guest-escape flaw prompts cloud fleet mitigations ⚠️  AWS disclosed CVE-2026-122192, a Firecracker flaw that can let a guest-root attacker access virtual-machine monitor memory under specific snapshot and device conditions.  Fly.io says it has deployed fleet-wide mitigations and additional updates may gradually restart Machines. AWS says its own services, including Lambda, are unaffected.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Affects Firecracker 0.23.0–1.16.1 when VMs are restored from snapshots using the File memory backend with a balloon or virtio-mem device; fixed in 1.16.2 and 1.17.0. No malicious exploitation has been reported.  aws.amazon.com/security/secu… #CyberSecurity #CloudSecurity

🏨 🚨 16M HOTEL RESERVATION RECORDS WITH PAYMENT DATA ALLEGEDLY OFFERED FOR SALE  A threat actor on an underground forum claims to be selling about 16 million hotel reservation rows from a shared reservation-management dashboard used across thousands of hotels and fed by OTA (online travel agency) channels. No hotel group, OTA brand, or property-management vendor is named.  The actor claims the dataset includes: • Guest details • Booking and pricing data (check-in/out, room, amounts, OTA references) • A dedicated credit_card_details field • Pay-at-hotel, cancellation, no-show and modification metadata  Geography claimed: reservations mainly from the United States, United Kingdom, India, Philippines, Australia, Germany, Japan, France and Italy. The actor says new reservations with card information arrive daily and that the source will be disclosed only to buyers. None of this has been independently verified.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: If authentic, reservation plus card metadata is a ready kit for card-not-present fraud and highly credible booking-themed phishing. The missing vendor name makes containment harder for hotels and OTAs. Unverified threat-actor listing, NOT confirmation of a breach at any named company.  #DDW #DarkWeb #Hospitality #Hotels #DataLeak #PaymentCard #ThreatIntelligence

The listing allegedly includes: * A list of 5,000+ real estate consultants with names, phone numbers, email addresses and titles * Office names, rankings, review scores and years active * An office mapping list from a digital signature system (email, office name, region)  The claim has not been independently verified.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: If genuine, a full directory of agents with direct phone numbers is ideal material for targeted phishing, fake listing scams and impersonation of RE/MAX offices toward buyers and sellers. The digital signature mapping suggests access to internal tooling. Agents should be wary of unexpected requests for credentials or payments. Unverified threat-actor claim, NOT confirmation of a breach.  Source: this is for subscribers only. Whats up with all the AI buzzkillers god damn

Intel put so much pressure on us at Microsoft to use MMX instructions. First at the compiler level then "please just add some __asm to Office and Windows." It was dumb.  They used to explain how pasting an image into PowerPoint would be faster with MMX.

Some things I learned working at Microsoft:  1/ large numbers everywhere. $100M ARR service isn't even a footnote on executive slide decks. Leadership time is too valuable, come back when you're $1B+. Msft ecosystem is so rich that $1B+ sales are common (it's ludicrous how much work goes into closing these). Azure has ~250 services, some are a few mil and stagnant, others in hypergrowth, some are cash cows, you see every quadrant of the growth-share matrix. Imagine the imperial navy with ships of vastly different sizes as far the eye can see  2/ more on immense scale-- the smallest of Azure services run on 10K+ VMs. Large services run on 1M+ (some maybe 10M+ VMs, idk). Msft is stamping one new datacenter into the ground every four days (!!!!), a bewildering rate. Demand is so high, even with all this buildout we're forever capacity constrained. Azure brings in $100B in revenue and is growing 40%+ annually (at this size!!) There are ~225K msft employees. You almost have to think in scientific notation, 10^4 is a tiny number here  3/ msft is totalitarian re serving the customer. It's counterintuitive to outsiders, but the warts in msft products fall out of this culture. For example, it would be easy to improve the Azure Portal. But in all my time working with customers and partners here, I haven't heard even one person complain about the portal UI. Msft invests $0.00 dollars in anything that doesn't serve the customer and is completely unapologetic about downstream implications of this mindset  4/ msft can reshape itself overnight (when it has the will). People argued whether we waited too long to adapt after Storm-0558/Midnight Blizzard hacks (with the benefit of hindsight, we definitely did). But once the leadership team privileged security, everyone's job changed in two weeks. LT tied every engineer's comp to security, centralized reporting of embedded security teams, every org reshuffled its roadmap. Within days everyone was pushing PRs with security fixes. I would have thought it inconceivable to mobilize 200K+ employees this fast  5/ Azure is complicated. Postgres depends on compute, networking, AKS (or EKS for you aws people), secrets, etc. AKS depends on compute, networking, some datastore (probably Cosmos but idk), a dozen other things. Cosmos depends on... you get the idea. When anything breaks, everything above can break too. Some construction crew accidentally cuts a fiber cable in Brazil South, or a dedicated hardware compression chip browns out in storage, or compute failure rate in west eu spikes for some reason, or a million other failure modes. Msft is relentless about improving this, idk exactly but fully loaded probably 50% of engineer time goes into resilience  6/ re lifers who work 20+ years here, SV sneers at this but I now see it differently. I was once on the bridge debugging some IO issue, we call storage, the guy diagnoses it in about a minute, we chitchat, turns out he built NT asyncio support. Or same story but with networking, the guy built NT tcp/ip stack. I used to have a boss here, we were bumping into some problem, she casually goes oh yeah, we hit that when I was working on .NET bytecode. The ex-DEC VAX/VMS database engineers built SQL Server, some are still here. I love bumping into these people  7/ I never *really* understood distribution until I got here. As an example, our team had a customer in Seoul w/ a deep performance problem. We had to fix it to unlock one of these giant contracts. We don't speak Korean, they don't speak English. Of course msft has specialists in Seoul who get to the customer site before you could even get on a plane. There is an office in every major city, a relationship with every major entity, legal experts in every jurisdiction. You can reach these ppl instantly. Claude tells me msft has ~180 offices in ~100 countries (!!) U.S. government has ~270 consulates in ~170 countries. So msft outposts aren't quite as vast as U.S. diplomatic network, but pretty vast  8/ in the 90s everyone was afraid of msft. The lore is that BillG was ruthless. He'd clone you, beat you via ecosystem/distribution strength, and moreover make the ecosystem stronger with the new product. I wasn't there to compare, but msft of today is ruthless about winning, has the will to adapt, and has the wherewithal to undertake colossal projects. Ppl see Teams bugs or whatever and completely misread the signals. Teams is less polished than Slack because msft doesn't care one iota about polish. It cares about winning, and is frighteningly good at it. Underestimate at your own risk

🚨 New Android vulnerability can trap phones in endless boot loops without app permissions Security researchers at Bitdefender have discovered a serious Android vulnerability, dubbed GhostMap, that allows a malicious app to render a smartphone unusable simply by being installed. The app requires no permissions, contains no executable code, and never needs to be opened. The flaw exploits how Android processes specially crafted APK files, causing a critical system service to repeatedly crash and restart. The resulting boot loop can persist even in Safe Mode, potentially forcing victims to perform a factory reset and lose locally stored data. Researchers successfully demonstrated the attack on a Google Pixel 10 running Android 17, observing 110 consecutive crashes during testing. The vulnerability was also reproduced on Android versions dating back to Android 10. Bitdefender reported the issue to Google in August 2026, but Google classified it as outside the scope of a security update. No patch is currently available. Although researchers have not observed the persistent boot-loop attack being exploited in the wild, the vulnerability raises concerns about attackers using malicious applications to disable devices or demand payment to prevent data loss. Source: https://www. bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/lab s/ghostmap-android

### 1. 현재 주요 사이버보안 트렌드
최근 보안 위협은 기존의 핵심 시스템 직접 공격에서 벗어나 백엔드 API, 위탁 SaaS, 웹 서비스 등 외곽 접점을 노리는 공격이 주류를 이루고 있습니다([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/96187/)). 특히 생성형 AI를 활용한 공격 기법이 고도화되어, 자동화된 취약점 탐색 및 악성코드 유포에 AI 모델이 적극적으로 악용되는 추세입니다([Check Point Research](https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/hacking-on-autopilot-inside-artex-cybercrime-campaigns/)). 또한, 공급망 공격의 일환으로 백업 서비스나 관리형 솔루션의 취약점을 이용한 대규모 데이터 유출 사례가 빈번하게 발생하고 있습니다([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209352)).

### 2. 주요 위협 행위자 / 캠페인
- **Storm-2603**: [Securelist](https://securelist.com/storm-2603-fileless-toolshell-attack/121467/) - SharePoint 환경을 대상으로 ToolShell을 악용한 파일리스(fileless) 공격 수행.
- **SlippyNunchucks**: [WeLiveSecurity](https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/slippynunchucks-hijacks-sogou-input-methods-brand-promotion-mechanism-to-distribute-malware/) - Sogou Input Method의 브랜드 프로모션 메커니즘을 하이재킹하여 악성코드 유포.
- **Gorbag**: [WeLiveSecurity](https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gorbag-orcs-border-harvesting-intelligence-ukraine/) - 러시아 연계 그룹으로, 우크라이나 조직을 대상으로 정보 탈취형 악성코드(infostealer) 유포.

### 3. 한국 관련 위협
- **더존비즈온 APO 백업서비스 침해사고**: KAC공항서비스, 전남정보문화산업진흥원 등 다수 기관에서 개인정보 유출 가능성 공지([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209352), [데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209350)).
- **한국공인중개사협회**: 교육원 서버 해킹으로 인한 회원 개인정보 유출 가능성 조사 중([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209351)).
- **C3RB3R 랜섬웨어**: 시놀로지(Synology) NAS를 타겟으로 한 랜섬웨어 공격 국내외 보고([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5792)).

### 4. 주요 CVE / 취약점
- **CVE-2026-83844**: Microsoft Paint RCE, Microsoft Store를 통한 수동 업데이트 필요([TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/microsoft-paint-rce-fix-now-available.html)).
- **CVE-2026-109618 / 109619**: PHP RCE, 전 세계 웹 서버 및 CMS 대상 심각한 취약점([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/)).
- **CVE-2026-98432**: Linux Kernel IPv4 TCP UAF, 원격 코드 실행 가능([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5792)).
- **CVE-2026-63017**: Subnet Solutions PowerSYSTEM Center SQL Injection([CISA ICS](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-307-01)).

### 5. IOC 요약
- **CVE**:

    - CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 ([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/), [Qualys](https://blog.qualys.com/category/product-tech))
    - CVE-2026-98432 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5792))
    - CVE-2026-63017 ([CISA ICS](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-307-01))

- **Microsoft Paint 업데이트**: Windows Update가 아닌 Microsoft Store를 통해 최신 버전으로 즉시 업데이트 수행.

- **백업 서버 보안 강화**: 더존비즈온 등 위탁 백업 서비스 이용 기관은 해당 업체의 보안 공지를 확인하고, 접근 제어 및 로그 모니터링 강화.
